To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Na+-K+-ATPase accounts for 40% of the total cerebral metabolism in the EEG-arrested brain.

(1) the barbiturate EEG flat is not associated with an absolute minimum in cerebral metabolism; (2) a large fraction of metabolism is not related to synaptic transmission; (3) a large fraction may be related to Na +-K+ transport; (4) Na+-K+ pump activity may be reduced by 40%; (5) the remaining 60% of metabolism is related to processes not identified by the present study.
Cerebral metabolism may be reduced to 60% of control values by barbiturate anesthesia and by inhibiting Na+-K+ pump activity with ouabain."
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relation between Na-K transport and metabolism in brain.
the relation of cerebral metabolism to Na+-K+-ATPase and Na+-K+ fluxes in the canine brain in vivo.
a quantitative description of the relation between Na+ and K+ transport, energy metabolism, and synaptic transmission in the canine cerebral cortex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Na+-K+-ATPase is an energy consuming process which is not the only source of energy consumption in the brain.
Na+-K+ pump and leak fluxes account for 20-40% of the metabolism of an EEG-arrested brain and that this fraction is independent of the metabolic state of the brain.
40% of the metabolism in barbiturate inhibited EEG-arrested canine brain can be related to Na +-K+ transport.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Na+-K+ ATPase is the rate-limiting factor for the energy consumption in the brain.
the barbiturate minimum of cerebral metabolism is not a constant, but varies with the level of Na+-K+ fluxes and the metabolic demand for Na+- K+ transport.
40-60% of metabolism is related to the maintenance of Na+-K+ gradients and that this is reduced to 20-40% of metabolism by barbiturate inhibition of Na+-K-ATPase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Na+-K+-ATPase can be inhibited to a significant extent without affecting cerebral metabolism.
the barbiturate minimum may be reduced by 40% by blocking Na+-K+ fluxes with ouabain.
the barbiturate minimum is not the minimum for brain metabolism.
